source_read: PDF of scanned print pages, Lancet 340, pp. 384-387 (all pages; the text layer omits Tables I-IV, so every number was read on pages rendered at 150 and 300 dpi)

claims.overstatement: Henry's part is accurate. Two wording points. (1) The closing sentence 'None of these studies measured MDMA in living people after ordinary use' should acknowledge that Henry gives single plasma values in living people seen after use: 5 survivors of severe complications after 1 to 3 tablets or capsules (one a child after accidental ingestion), 0.2-0.97 mg/L (Table II), and 3 survivors of road accidents, 0.05-0.34 mg/L (Table III). These are selected hospital presentations, not ordinary use, but they overlap the fatal values (0.11-1.26 mg/L) and strengthen the claim's overlap point. (2) Henry's values are plasma (column header), apparently from hospital samples before death at unstated times; they are not post-mortem femoral blood and are not like-for-like with the Sheffield values.
claims.note: All numbers checked on 300 dpi renders: ages 16-21 (5 men, 2 women); reported amounts 3, 2, 5 and 1 tablets, 3 tablets, tablets of unstated number, and none stated (found collapsed after a party); settings club, party, pop concert; temperatures 40-43 C; plasma MDMA 0.36, 0.424, 0.11, 1.16, 1.26 mg/L (0.11-1.26 in 5; detected without a value in 2); the person with 7.72 mg/L allegedly took 42 tablets at home. Deaths came 2.5 h to 60 h after admission, one after a liver transplant (graft rejection, 18 days). Cases came from enquiries to the National Poisons Information Service and National Poisons Unit laboratory records; 2 of the 7 deaths were already published, and samples in cases 1-4 were analysed in other laboratories. The paper also reports two deaths from injuries in road accidents with plasma MDMA 0.1 and 0.13 mg/L (Table III), inside the range of the fatal toxicity cases.

anchors.extracted: All enquiries to the National Poisons Information Service in London about suspected ecstasy or MDMA use recorded January 1990 to December 1991; clinical details and outcome requested from the hospital and, where appropriate, the pathologist or coroner; National Poisons Unit laboratory records searched for samples in which ecstasy was mentioned or detected.

anchors.locator: Table I (fatal cases of MDMA toxicity) and footnote
anchors.extracted: 7 deaths, ages 16-21 (5 male, 2 female); 3, 2, 5 and 1 tablets, tablets of unstated number, none stated, 3 tablets; at a club, parties, after a party, a pop concert; temperatures 41.8, 41, 42.1, 40, 41, 40, 43 C; plasma MDMA 0.36, detected, detected (blood and urine), 0.424, 0.11, 1.16 (with MDA 0.06 and amphetamine 0.10), 1.26 mg/L; died 2.5 h to 60 h after admission, one 18 days after a liver transplant; time of sampling not stated; cases 1-4 analysed in other laboratories; footnote says no ethanol or other drugs except low amphetamine in case 5 (the table shows it in case 6).
One analytically documented overdose, allegedly 42 tablets taken at home, plasma MDMA 7.72 mg/L, with no symptoms beyond a hangover, plus tachycardia and hypertension.
Amounts were hard to establish, but in most cases only a few tablets or capsules were taken, and the toxicity did not seem to result from overdose.

5 people who survived severe complications (ages 1-25; 1-3 tablets or capsules, one a 1-year-old after accidental ingestion of one tablet): plasma MDMA 0.2 (with amphetamine 0.1), 0.7, 0.97 (MDA 0.05), 0.24 (MDA 0.02, amphetamine 0.02, MDEA in urine), 0.21 mg/L, i.e. 0.2-0.97, overlapping the fatal 0.11-1.26.

anchors.locator: Table III (road traffic accident victims) and footnote
anchors.extracted: MDMA identified in 5 people in four road accidents: 2 died of injuries (multiple fractures; multiple skull fractures) with plasma MDMA 0.1 and 0.13 mg/L; 3 survived with 0.05, 0.34 and 0.15 mg/L; ethanol not detected in any.

The authors put the deaths down to heatstroke with disseminated intravascular coagulation; all fatal cases were at crowded parties or clubs and already had established heatstroke when first seen; they conclude the acute toxicity pattern may be due mainly to the circumstances of use, not to the amount taken.

reporting_issues.note: Same discrepancy found independently in step 1.
Confirmed on the 300 dpi figure: monthly calls in 1991 were 7, 19, 23, 14, 35 and 26 in January-June (editors' approximate reading), so the rise began in February 1991, not in the second half.

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with high overall: cases assembled from calls and samples to one service without inclusion rules, denominators or sampling times.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is fair: the conclusion that the toxicity pattern is due mainly to circumstances, and the hepatotoxicity attribution, go beyond what was recorded.

missed: Tables II and III (p. 386) against Table I (p. 385): the five survivors of severe complications had plasma MDMA 0.2-0.97 mg/L and the two people who died of injuries in road accidents had 0.1 and 0.13 mg/L, all inside the range of the fatal toxicity cases (0.11-1.26 mg/L). The card holds these values (exposure field) but does not state the comparison, which is the paper's most direct evidence that plasma level did not separate deaths from survivors; it bears on cl_mdma_deaths_fatal_level, whose closing sentence says no study measured MDMA in living people after ordinary use.
